caption:
Were the Fox sisters real mediums? No — one of them stood on a stage and showed how the trick worked.

In 1848, in Hydesville, New York, two young sisters, Catherine (Kate) and Margaretta (Maggie) Fox, reported rappings in a house the neighbours already believed was haunted. Their older sister Leah took charge of them and managed their careers. On 14 November 1849 they demonstrated their rapping at Corinthian Hall in Rochester — the first spiritualist demonstration before a paying public. Séances followed for hundreds of people; William Lloyd Garrison, James Fenimore Cooper and Sojourner Truth were among those who attended in New York in 1850.

Doubts came early. Investigators from the University at Buffalo concluded in 1851 that the raps were made by cracking joints, and would not occur with cushions under the sisters' feet. A relative, Mrs Norman Culver, signed a statement saying she had helped by touching them to signal when to rap. The physicist William Crookes examined Kate between 1871 and 1874 and declared the raps genuine.

On 21 October 1888, before 2,000 people at the New York Academy of Music, Maggie produced raps at will while doctors came on stage to confirm the sound came from her toe joints. A reporter had offered $1,500. She retracted the confession a year later, saying it had been forced from her by money and by enemies of Spiritualism — and the paper never paid in full. Both sisters resumed paid séances and died in extreme poverty, Kate in 1892, Maggie in 1893.

Still unresolved: which version of Maggie's story to believe. Spiritualism kept growing either way.

Images: N. Currier lithograph after a daguerreotype by Appleby, 1852; a framed portrait of the three sisters; Kate Fox photographed by Gurney; an unidentified Fox sister in a gold oval frame; and a braided lock of Kate's hair. All public domain.
